Gordon Robin was born in Melbourne, Australia, on 17 January 1921 and educated at Wesley College in Melbourne
He went on to the University of Melbourne, where he read physics, gaining a Master's Degree in 1942.
He joined the Royal Australian Naval Voluntary Reserve immediately upon graduating and was commissioned as a sub-lieutenant.

Promoted lieutenant, he joined HMS Stygian, which towards the end of World War II sailed in support of a midget submarine (XE3) to attack Japanese cruisers in the Jahore Straits and Singapore harbour.
Robin demobilised in the United Kingdom, against standing orders, and went on to study nuclear physics at Birmingham University, under Professor (later Sir Mark) Oliphant, in his cyclotron project.

This led to an offer of a year (1947–48) as base commander at Signy Island in the South Orkneys with the Falkland Islands Dependencies Survey (FIDS)
Returning from Signy, Robin rejoined the Physics Department at Birmingham and the cyclotron project, gaining a lectureship in October 1948.

But in 1949, with his appetite for the Antarctic already whetted, a new opportunity arose and he was recruited to the Norwegian–British–Swedish Antarctic Expedition as third-in-command and physicist in charge of the seismic survey to measure ice thickness.

In early 1957 Robin returned to Australia to the Australian National University to work on ocean waves
He accepted and arrived in Cambridge in 1958, becoming the first person to hold a full-time post heading a department in polar science in a British university and arguably the world.

He secured substantial financial support from the Ford Foundation, which, along with assistance from the University of Cambridge and other donors, was sufficient to make a start on the SPRI 'extension' in 1966.
Working together, Robin and Evans pioneered the effective development of the radio echo sounding (RES) technique to measure ice thickness.
The first continuous airborne radio echo soundings were made in Ellesmere Island in 1966 using a DHC-3 Otter by Robin, Evans, and Geoffrey Hattersley-Smith of the Canadian Defence Research Board.
In 1967 Robin initiated a 12-year collaborative programme with the US National Science Foundation to map and glaciologically explore the Antarctic ice sheet
